# Hours, Output and the Pilot Problem: A Re-examination of the Halden Reduced-Hours Pilot

*Comment, Journal of Labour and Organisation Studies. K. Varga and T. Holm, Centre for Applied Labour Statistics.*

## Abstract

The Halden pilot reported that 61 organisations maintained output while cutting scheduled hours by 20%, implying a 23.4% gain in output per hour. Using the pilot's microdata, released under the Institute's data-sharing policy, we re-examine the result. Four problems, each documented below, account for most of the reported gain: attrition that was not random, a manager-reported output measure that overstates output relative to organisations' own records, an hours denominator that counts scheduled rather than actual time, and an unadjusted revenue comparison. Correcting the first three, the gain in output per hour falls from 23.4% to 10.8% in the subset of organisations where correction is possible. We then argue that the remaining gain is plausibly a novelty effect, and that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty.

## 1. Attrition

The working paper states that nine of the 70 enrolled organisations "withdrew during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons". The microdata tell a different story. Seven of the nine withdrew after the reduced schedule had begun: four in the first month and three in the second. In exit forms, six of the nine gave workload or inability to maintain output as the main reason, and two gave scheduling. The organisations that found the change hardest were therefore removed from the sample before the outcome was measured. With nine of 70 organisations missing, and those nine plausibly the least successful, the reported sample of 61 is a sample of survivors.

## 2. The output measure

The primary outcome was an index completed by a manager who was also the pilot's internal sponsor. Managers were asked to base the index on organisational records, but were not required to submit them. Twenty-three organisations did submit underlying records (billable hours delivered, tickets closed, units produced, or cases completed). For these 23 we can compare the manager's index with the index implied by the records.

**Table 1. Manager-reported and record-based output, 23 organisations with records**

| Measure | Mean output index (baseline = 100) |
|---|---|
| Manager-reported index | 98.9 |
| Index computed from submitted records | 95.1 |
| Difference | −3.8 points |

In 19 of the 23 organisations the manager-reported index exceeded the record-based index. We do not suggest bad faith. A manager responsible for a change he or she advocated, asked to rate its effect on a scale where 100 means "unchanged", will tend to round toward success. But the difference is systematic, and the headline output figure of 98.7 should not be taken at face value.

## 3. The hours denominator

The pilot computed output per hour by dividing output by the ratio of scheduled hours, 0.8. Twenty-seven organisations used time-tracking software throughout. Their data show average actual weekly hours of 40.3 at baseline and 34.6 during the pilot, a fall of 14.1% rather than 20%. The difference comes from two sources visible in the logs: longer working days on the remaining four days (average +0.7 hours per day), and work logged on the scheduled day off (on average 1.6 hours per week). Some further work on the day off is probably not logged.

Seventeen organisations have both submitted output records and time tracking. In this subset, record-based output was 95.4 and actual hours fell from 40.4 to 34.8 (−13.9%). The implied gain in output per actual hour is 10.8% (95.4 / 86.1), less than half the reported 23.4%.

**Table 2. Implied gain in output per hour under successive corrections**

| Specification | Output | Hours ratio | Gain per hour |
|---|---|---|---|
| As reported (all 61) | 98.7 | 0.800 | +23.4% |
| Record-based output, scheduled hours (23) | 95.1 | 0.800 | +18.9% |
| Manager-reported output, actual hours (27) | 98.4 | 0.859 | +14.6% |
| Record-based output, actual hours (17) | 95.4 | 0.861 | +10.8% |

## 4. Revenue

The working paper reports revenue 1.4% higher than in the previous year. This is a nominal comparison. Consumer prices rose by 4.1% over the same twelve months; in real terms, revenue in participating organisations fell by approximately 2.6%. Revenue is in any case a poor proxy for productivity, but the figure as presented gives a misleading impression of growth.

## 5. Sectoral claims

The pilot concluded that gains in output per hour were "found in every sector" and that the model is "sector-general". This conclusion is an artifact of the per-hour metric. When hours are cut by 20%, any output index above 80 will register as a per-hour gain. Retail and hospitality output fell by 6.9% on the manager-reported measure; the three retail and hospitality organisations among the 23 with records show a fall of 11.2%. A fall in output of this size in a customer-facing business is not evidence that reduced hours work there. The Varden County trial's counter and contact-centre stratum, the only randomised evidence on coverage-bound work, found a fall in output per employee of 11.4% and longer waits for the public. That is, in our view, the most reliable finding in the literature to date.

## 6. Novelty

After the corrections above, a gain in output per actual hour of about 11% remains in the subset of survivors with usable data. We think this residual should not be read as a durable effect. The pilot's own survey shows self-reported energy at work rising by 0.61 standard deviations at month three and falling to 0.29 at month six. Extrapolating this decline, energy would return to baseline at around month ten. A change that staff chose, welcomed and knew to be under evaluation is the classic setting for a novelty effect: effort rises while the change is new and observed, and falls back once it is routine. Six months is not long enough to distinguish a novelty effect from a durable one, and the burden of proof lies with those claiming the latter.

## 7. The meetings hypothesis

The Varden trial's authors report, in an unregistered exploratory analysis, that cuts in recurring meetings correlated with per-hour gains across seven treated offices, and suggest this as a mechanism. We regard this as a post hoc account fitted to a subgroup. A correlation across seven offices, selected for analysis after the results were known, is precisely the kind of finding that does not replicate. The meetings explanation has an intuitive appeal that has outrun its evidence, and it should not be cited as a mechanism.

## 8. Conclusion

Taking the problems together: attrition removed the organisations least able to cope; the output measure overstated output by roughly four points; the hours measure overstated the reduction in time by roughly six points; and the remaining gain coincides with a decaying measure of enthusiasm. We conclude that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the best-supported finding is the negative one: where output depends on presence, reduced hours reduce output.

We recommend that future evaluations use record-based output, actual hours, a randomised or at least matched comparison group, follow-up of at least eighteen months, and analysis of all enrolled organisations including those that withdraw.

## Data note

All re-analyses use the Halden pilot microdata (release 1.2). The corrections in Table 2 can only be computed for subsets of organisations, and those subsets were not chosen at random; organisations with time tracking and records may differ from the others. Our corrected estimates therefore describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole.

response:
The Comment's empirical sections are a real contribution: the attrition finding especially, and the record-versus-manager comparison. But its conclusion goes well beyond its own numbers. The corrections leave a per-hour gain of about 11% in the subset where they can be computed. The argument that this residual is novelty is the weakest part of the paper. And "entirely an artifact" is contradicted by the Varden trial, which the Comment itself calls the most reliable evidence.

## What holds up

- **Attrition (§1).** This is the most important finding. Halden described the nine withdrawals as happening "during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons". The microdata show instead that seven left after the schedule began, and six cited workload or output. Halden needs to correct this, and its continuation rate should be restated against all 70 enrolled organisations: 56 of 70 is 80%, not 92%.
- **Manager versus record-based output (§2).** The manager index exceeded the record-based index in 19 of 23 organisations. A sign test on that split gives p ≈ 0.001, so the bias is systematic rather than noise.
- **Arithmetic.** Table 2 reproduces correctly: 98.7/0.8, 95.1/0.8, 98.4/0.859 and 95.4/0.861. The hours ratios match the stated hours, and the real-revenue figure checks (1.014/1.041 ≈ −2.6%).
- **Sectoral critique (§5).** This makes the same point I raised about Halden: any output index above 80 registers as a per-hour gain, so "found in every sector" was guaranteed.

## Main problems

### 1. The abstract claims an attrition correction that was never made

The abstract says "correcting the first three [problems]" brings the gain to 10.8%, and the first of the three is attrition. But Table 2 corrects only output and hours. The 10.8% is computed among survivors, as §6 and the Data note themselves say.

Attrition probably biases the estimate upward, so 10.8% is better described as an upper bound for this subset. Better still, the authors could bound it. If the withdrawers have any output data in the microdata, Lee bounds or worst-case imputation are possible. Otherwise the abstract should simply be reworded.

### 2. Table 2 changes the sample and the correction at the same time

Each row uses a different set of organisations: 61, then 23, 27 and 17. So the fall from 23.4% to 10.8% mixes the effect of the corrections with differences in sample composition. Organisations with time tracking and submitted records are probably weighted towards software and professional services.

What's needed is the uncorrected figure for the same 17 organisations: their manager index divided by 0.8. Only that comparison isolates what the corrections do.

Related gaps:
- No uncertainty is reported for any corrected estimate. With 17 organisations, the 10.8% needs an interval.
- Halden used employee-weighted means, and the Comment doesn't say how its means are weighted.

### 3. The hours breakdown doesn't reconcile

§3 attributes the extra hours to two sources:
- +0.7 hours per day over four days, which is 2.8 hours;
- 1.6 hours logged on the day off.

Starting from 32 scheduled hours, that implies about 36.4 hours a week, or about 36.6 using the 8.06-hour baseline day. The reported figure is 34.6. If the 0.7 is actually per week, the numbers fit: 32 + 0.7 + 1.6 ≈ 34.3, close to the reported figure. One of the figures is wrong.

### 4. The novelty argument is weak

- **The extrapolation arithmetic is off.** Energy fell from 0.61 SD to 0.29 SD between months 3 and 6, a drop of about 0.107 SD per month. Continuing linearly, it reaches zero at about month 8.7, not "around month ten". In any case, extrapolating linearly from two points is not a trend.
- **Energy is not output.** Self-reported energy falling is not evidence that productivity fell.
- **The direct test is available but not run.** Halden collected the output index *monthly*, and the Comment has the microdata. If the per-hour gain is novelty, output should decline across months 1–6, especially in the record-based subset. Showing that would be far stronger than extrapolating a survey measure.
- **The "burden of proof" framing doesn't establish anything.** "Six months cannot distinguish novelty from a durable effect" is a fair reason for caution. It is not grounds for concluding the effect is novelty.

### 5. "Entirely an artifact" contradicts the evidence the Comment cites

The Varden trial was designed to avoid exactly the problems the Comment documents in Halden:
- offices were randomised, so there was no self-selection;
- output came from administrative records rather than manager ratings;
- hours came from timesheets;
- results are reported at nine months.

It still found per-hour gains of +12.5% in case-processing and +6.7% in counter offices. Neither interval includes zero.

The Comment calls Varden's counter stratum "the most reliable finding in the literature", yet it ignores the case-processing result and the per-hour gains in both strata. A novelty effect remains possible at Varden, since staff knew their assignment. But Varden's staff did not choose the change, and the controls knew a trial was running.

The defensible conclusion is narrower: the Halden headline is substantially inflated, and the durability of the remaining gain is unknown. The current wording also generalises from one pilot to "reduced-hours schemes" as a whole, and it conflicts with the abstract's own "account for *most* of the reported gain".

### 6. The meetings section misdescribes the Varden analysis

- **The seven offices were not "selected after the results were known".** They are all the treated case-processing offices. The calendar data were collected in month six, at managers' request, before the nine-month outcomes existed.
- **Varden did not present meetings as an established mechanism.** It said a reduction in meetings "may account for part" of the gain, stated that seven offices "cannot establish a mechanism", and registered a confirmatory test. The Comment is attacking a stronger claim than the one Varden made.
- **The hypothesis is not purely post hoc.** Halden's own manager interviews named meetings as the most common change (47 of 58). A simple accounting of Varden's figures also suggests that time freed from meetings could account for most of the per-hour gain.

The fair criticism is that the evidence is thin and unconfirmed. That differs from saying the hypothesis "should not be cited as a mechanism".

## Smaller points

- **Record-based output isn't automatically the truth.** Records may capture a narrower slice of output than the manager's overall judgement, for example billable hours only. The direction of the gap is persuasive, but its size depends on how comparable the records are. One sentence on this would help.
- **The retail sample is tiny.** The −11.2% for retail and hospitality comes from three organisations and needs that caveat.
- **CPI is a rough deflator.** Deflating with sector output prices would be better. The conclusion that real revenue fell probably holds either way.
- **Exit reasons don't add up.** Six cited workload, two cited scheduling, and the ninth isn't accounted for.
- **The Data note is good but sits at the end.** Its caveat that the corrected estimates "describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole" should be reflected in the abstract and conclusion.

## Overall

As a re-analysis, the Comment establishes that Halden's 23.4% is inflated by misreported attrition, optimistic manager ratings and a scheduled-hours denominator. The best available correction puts the gain at about 11% among survivors, with some upward bias still left in. That is a solid, publishable finding.

The final step, from "smaller and uncertain" to "entirely an artifact", is not supported. Across the three papers, the evidence points to:
- per-hour gains that are real but much smaller than voluntary pilots report;
- falls in output per employee where output depends on staff being present;
- open questions about how long the gains last and what drives them.

The 24-month Varden follow-up, and a month-by-month analysis of the Halden microdata, are the obvious next tests.
